prompt: Why can the nightly job read the day's sales in any order, as many times as it likes?
hint: What is true of yesterday at two in the morning?

choices.text: Its period is over
choices.why: Right. At two in the morning nobody is still selling yesterday.

choices.text: It runs on a faster machine than the shops
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; the input is fixed because the day is over.

choices.text: The warehouse sorts the sales before the job starts
choices.why: The warehouse is where the job writes, not something that prepares its input.

choices.text: Each shop sends one file, already in order
choices.why: Even unordered files would do: the point is that nothing more will arrive.

prompt: The batch runs every five minutes instead of every night. What has it still not become?

choices.text: A cheaper pipeline than the nightly one, since each run is small
choices.why: It is dearer: 288 starts a day, each re-reading its sources.

choices.text: A program that handles each sale as it arrives
choices.why: Right. It still waits for a period to close; only the period got shorter.

choices.text: A pipeline that answers questions about today rather than yesterday
choices.why: It does answer about today, five minutes late. What it is not is a stream.

choices.text: A job that a late file delays
choices.why: It still is one: a late file delays the next run, as the table says.

prompt: Somebody says streaming is just batch run very often, so the hard part is speed. Which answer to them is the section's?

choices.text: Speed is hard too, but modern brokers solve it
choices.why: The section calls speed the easy part.

choices.text: Batch and streaming need different storage engines and file formats, and that is where the real difficulty lies
choices.why: Storage comes up in lesson 2, but it is not the argument here.

choices.text: The period never closes, so completeness, reruns and order each need an answer of their own
choices.why: Right. Those are the questions a batch answers for free.

choices.text: Running jobs very often is impossible, so a stream is the only option
choices.why: Running often is possible, just expensive; that is the table's point.

prompt: Match each thing that changes to the lessons that deal with it.

pairs.right: event time and late data, lessons 9 to 11
operating and paying for it, lessons 16 and 17

prompt: A till loses its connection at 10:20 and sends its sales at 14:00. A program counts sales per minute by the time each one arrived. What is wrong with its 14:00 minute?

choices.text: Nothing, because arrival time is the time of the sale
choices.why: Here they are almost four hours apart.

choices.text: It is missing the sales that arrived at 14:00
choices.why: They are there; the trouble is what else is there.

choices.text: Hours of Natal's earlier sales are in it
choices.why: Right. Counting by processing time puts them where they arrived.

choices.text: It counts each sale from Natal twice over
choices.why: Nothing is duplicated; the sales are in the wrong minute.

prompt: When a sale happened is its event time; when the program saw it is its ___ time.
How far a stream processor has fallen behind the events it reads is called ___.
Kafka keeps the order of a deposit and a withdrawal. Under which condition, according to the section?

choices.text: Always, for every message in a topic, whatever its key or partition
choices.why: Order is narrower than that: per key, inside one partition.

choices.text: When both carry the same key and so land in one partition
choices.why: Right. Per key, inside one partition, and nowhere else.

choices.text: Only when the topic has a single consumer reading it
choices.why: The number of readers does not create or destroy the order in which things are stored.

choices.text: When they arrive within the same second
choices.why: Timing is not what Kafka orders by.

prompt: Which of these requests does the section say a stream serves better than a batch? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Blocking a card used in two countries ten minutes apart
choices.why: Yes: an answer tomorrow is after the money has gone.

choices.text: The stock count shown on the website
choices.why: Yes: a promise that depends on the current state.

choices.text: A weekly report the manager reads on Monday
choices.why: The period closes, and a complete number beats a fresh one.

choices.text: Training a model on last year's sales
choices.why: The input is finite and fixed.

choices.text: A figure an auditor has to reproduce from a file
choices.why: The auditor wants it reproducible, not live.

prompt: Ponto Final's sales reach the stock system, the loyalty points, the warehouse and the accountant, and none of them is in a hurry. Why might it still adopt Kafka?

choices.text: One sale in a log is read by all four
choices.why: Right. That reason is about integration, not speed.

choices.text: Kafka makes each of the four systems process the sales faster
choices.why: None of them is in a hurry, so speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Kafka replaces the warehouse and the nightly job
choices.why: The warehouse stays; it becomes one of the log's readers.

choices.text: Kafka is cheaper than any nightly job
choices.why: The section says the reverse: it costs all the time.

prompt: What arrangement does the section call the usual answer, rather than one or the other?

choices.text: A batch every five minutes, which is close enough to a stream anyway
choices.why: That is the shrinking batch from the first section, not the arrangement here.

choices.text: One log; urgent readers now, a batch at night
choices.why: Right. The stream is the source and the batch is one of its readers.

choices.text: Two separate pipelines from the tills, one fast and one slow
choices.why: Two pipelines from the source is exactly what the log avoids.

choices.text: Stream for everything
choices.why: The batch stays, as one reader of the log.

prompt: Why is a virtual machine the recommended path for this course?

choices.text: The servers the course installs stay inside a machine you delete in one command
choices.why: Right. A database, a broker and three engines are better kept apart.

choices.text: Kafka only runs inside virtual machines
choices.why: Kafka runs on any Linux with Java; the installed path works too.

choices.text: The transcripts in the lessons would not match on an Ubuntu installed directly on a computer
choices.why: The table says they match on all three paths.

choices.text: A virtual machine is faster than the computer it runs on
choices.why: It is not; the reason is isolation.

prompt: How many gigabytes of memory does the course ask the virtual machine to have?
Before unpacking Kafka, the lesson compares two long strings. What does it prove when they are equal?

choices.text: That the file was downloaded from a fast mirror
choices.why: The address is archive.apache.org, chosen because it keeps every release.

choices.text: That Java is installed and can run Kafka
choices.why: The checksum says nothing about Java.

choices.text: That the file is Apache's, whole
choices.why: Right. A cut-short download or another file gives a different hash.

choices.text: That the archive unpacks without errors
choices.why: Unpacking is the next step; the hash is about the bytes downloaded.

prompt: You ran the `echo` line that adds Kafka to `PATH`, and in the same shell `kafka-topics.sh` is still not found. Why?

choices.text: The download of Kafka failed halfway and left the directory empty
choices.why: Then `tar` would have failed first.

choices.text: The shell started before the line was added
choices.why: Right. `source ~/.profile` or a new shell fixes it.

choices.text: The virtual environment must be activated first
choices.why: The course puts its `bin` on the PATH instead of activating it.

choices.text: `kafka-topics.sh` needs `sudo`
choices.why: Nothing in the course runs Kafka as root.

prompt: In `cluster.sh`, node 3 takes client connections on which port?

choices.why: That is node 1: 9091 + 1.
That is node 2's controller port, 9191 + 2.
That is node 3's controller port, not the one clients use.

prompt: What does `cluster.sh start` wait for before it says a node is up?

choices.text: A connection on the node's port
choices.why: Right. Started is not ready; answering is.

choices.text: The Java process to appear in the process list
choices.why: That only says it started, not that it is ready.

choices.text: A fixed ten seconds after the command
choices.why: It polls once a second, for at most sixty.

choices.text: The cluster id to be written to disk
choices.why: That happens during `new`, at format time.

prompt: In a node's directory there is `log` and there is `logs`. Where are the sales you send?

choices.text: In `logs`, beside what the node says about itself
choices.why: `logs` is the node's own diagnostic output.

choices.text: In `server.properties`
choices.why: That is the configuration the script generated.

choices.text: In `meta.properties`
choices.why: That holds the cluster id.

choices.text: In `log`, because Kafka stores a topic as a log
choices.why: Right. One letter of difference, and a different meaning.

prompt: The console consumer prints the five sales and does not return to the prompt. Why?

choices.text: It is still waiting for the sales that have not been sent yet
choices.why: Right. A stream has no end, so the reader waits.

choices.text: It crashed after the fifth message
choices.why: Ctrl+C ends it cleanly and it reports what it saw.

choices.text: It is writing the sales to disk
choices.why: The broker stores them; the consumer only reads.

choices.text: It needs `--max-messages` before it returns anything at all to the shell
choices.why: It works without it; that option only makes it stop.

prompt: After the first consumer is stopped, the same command prints nothing new. What makes the second run show the five sales?

choices.text: Sending the five sales again with `tills.py`
choices.why: That would add five more; the old ones are still there.

choices.text: Restarting the cluster
choices.why: A restart keeps what is on disk, and the consumer would still start at the end.

choices.text: Adding `--from-beginning`
choices.why: Right. Reading did not remove them.

choices.text: Creating the topic again
choices.why: It already exists, and making it again would not bring anything back.

prompt: In `tills.py`, why is `producer.flush()` called at the end?

choices.text: It deletes from memory the messages that were already sent
choices.why: It waits for them, it does not discard them.

choices.text: It waits for the broker to confirm every message
choices.why: Right. `produce` only hands the message to the client.

choices.text: It creates the sales topic if it does not exist yet
choices.why: The topic was made with `kafka-topics.sh` beforehand.

choices.text: It makes the next run start from the same seed
choices.why: The seed is an argument; flush is about delivery.

prompt: In `tills.py`, the shop is the message's ___, which decides where in the topic the sale is stored.
`./cluster.sh status` says `node 1: stopped` the morning after you shut the laptop. What do you run?

choices.text: `./cluster.sh new 1`, to rebuild the cluster
choices.why: That deletes the topics and their messages, which are still on disk.

choices.text: `./cluster.sh start`
choices.why: Right. The node is a process; its data is on disk.

choices.text: `multipass delete --purge stream`, and build again
choices.why: That is the last resort, not the first.

choices.text: Nothing: the cluster starts with the virtual machine
choices.why: The lesson says it does not start on its own.

prompt: Running a script prints a message naming `bash\r`. What happened to the file?

choices.text: It was saved with Windows line endings
choices.why: Right. `file` says CRLF and `sed` removes the extra character.

choices.text: It is not executable, because chmod was not run
choices.why: That gives a different message; the clue here is the `\r`.

choices.text: bash is not installed in the virtual machine
choices.why: bash is there; the name being looked for has a carriage return in it.

choices.text: The cluster is stopped
choices.why: The script never got far enough to look.

prompt: `cluster.sh start` says `port 9092 is taken by another program`. Why does the script check this before starting Java?

choices.text: Java refuses to start at all while any port on the machine is busy
choices.why: Java starts fine; the node fails later, when it tries to listen.

choices.text: Two Kafka nodes are allowed to share a port
choices.why: They cannot, and that is not what the check is for.

choices.text: Whoever holds it would answer the readiness test, and the node would die seconds later
choices.why: Right. The readiness test is a connection, which anybody holding the port would accept.

choices.text: Checking first makes the node come up faster, since Java skips its own test of the port
choices.why: It is about a clear error, not speed.

prompt: Put the steps of building the lab in the order the lesson takes them.
items: Install Java and the Python tools with apt-get

prompt: A colleague wants a live dashboard of yesterday's sales per shop, refreshed every second, for a meeting where the numbers are discussed once. What would the lesson tell them?

choices.text: Build it with Kafka, because fresh is always better
choices.why: Fresh is only worth it when somebody acts on the difference.

choices.text: Keep the nightly job: that day is over, and nobody acts on the difference
choices.why: Right. A complete number about a closed period is the batch's strength.

choices.text: Run the batch every second
choices.why: Yesterday does not change from one second to the next.

choices.text: Neither works for yesterday's data
choices.why: The batch is exactly for that.
